💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series.
  • 🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a upcoming image generation and editing model.
  • FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely fresh model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a upcoming image generation and editing model.

FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

Recent findings suggest that first, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:.

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

None of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

In a recent development, in Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:.

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

Recent findings suggest that A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Before you try out the following code snippets, make sure you have installed diffusers from main and have run hf auth login.

The above code snippet was tested on an H100, and it isn’t sufficient to run inference on it without CPU offloading. With CPU offloading enabled, this setup takes ~62GB to run.

Users who have access to Hopper-series GPUs can take advantage of Flash Attention 3 to speed up inference:.

You can check out the supported attention backends (we have many!) here.

Sources indicate that using bitsandbytes, we can load the transformer and text encoder models in 4-bit, allowing owners of 24GB GPUs to use the model locally. You can run this snippet on a GPU with ~20 GB of free VRAM.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

Due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

It has been revealed that ⚠️ To use the remote text encoder, you need to have a valid token. If you are already authenticated, no further action is needed.

The example below uses a combination of local and remote inference. Additionally, we quantize the DiT with NF4 quantization through bitsandbytes.

You can run this snippet on a GPU with 18 GB of VRAM:.

Industry observers note that for GPUs with even lower VRAM, we have group_offloading, which allows GPUs with as little as 8GB of free VRAM to use this model. However, you'll need 32GB of free RAM. Alternatively, if you're willing to sacrifice some speed, you can set low_cpu_mem_usage=True to reduce the RAM requirement to just 10GB.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space.

It has been revealed that FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

It has been revealed that FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):.

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):.

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:.

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

Sources indicate that being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

Many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

For this example, we’ll use multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset with the following configuration using FP8 training. Feel free to experiment more with the hyper-parameters and share your results 🤗.

The left image was generated using the pre-trained FLUX.2 model, and the right image was produced the LoRA.

In case your hardware isn’t compatible with FP8 training, you can use QLoRA with bitsandbytes. You first need to define a config.json file like so:.

And then pass its path to --bnb_quantization_config_path:.

Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020.
  • In a recent development, today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯.
  • The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020. Five years later, we now release v5.0.0rc-0.

In a recent development, today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯. Altogether, it has now surpassed 1.2 billion installs!

The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.

This growth is powered by the evolution of the field and the now mainstream access to AI. As a leading model-definition library in the ecosystem, we need to continuously evolve and adapt the library to continue being relevant. Reinvention is key for longevity in AI.

We’re fortunate to collaborate with many libraries and apps built on transformers, in no specific order: llama.cpp, MLX, onnxruntime, Jan, LMStudio, vLLM, SGLang, Unsloth, LlamaFactory, dLLM, MaxText, TensorRT, Argmax, among many other friends.

Industry observers note that for v5, we wanted to work on several notable aspects: simplicity, training, inference, and production. We detail the work that went into them in this post.

The first focus of the team was on simplicity. Working on transformers, we see the code as the product. We want our model integrations to be clean, so that the ecosystem may depend on our model definitions and understand what’s really happening under the hood, how models differ from each other, and the key features of each fresh model. Simplicity results in wider standardization, generality, and wider support.

Transformers is the backbone of hundreds of thousands of projects, Unsloth included. We build on Transformers to help people fine-tune and train models efficiently, whether that’s BERT, text-to-speech (TTS), or others; to run fast inference for reinforcement learning (RL) even when models aren’t yet supported in other libraries. We're excited for Transformers v5 and are super happy to be working with the Hugging Face team!

Transformers, at the core, remains a model architecture toolkit. We aim to have all recent architectures and to be the “source of truth” for model definitions. We’ve been adding between 1 - 3 fresh models every week for 5 years, shown in the timeline below:.

We’ve worked on improving that model-addition process.

Over the past year, we’ve heavily pushed our modular design as a significant step forward. This allows for easier maintenance, faster integration, and better collaboration across the community.

Industry observers note that we give a deeper overview in our Maintain the Unmaintainable blog post. For brevity, we aim to achieve a much easier model contribution process, as well as a lower maintenance burden. One metric we can highlight is that the number of lines of code to contribute (and review), drop significantly when modular is used:.

According to recent reports, while we respect the “One model, one file” philosophy, we continue introducing some abstractions making the management of common helpers simpler. The prime example of this is the introduction of the AttentionInterface, which offers a centralized abstraction for attention methods. The eager method will remain in the modeling file; others, such as FA1/2/3, FlexAttention, or SDPA, are moved to the interface.

Over the past couple of years, the increasing amount of 0-day support for new model architectures and standardization of attention handling has helped to simplify our support for post-training modern LLMs.

Sources indicate that we’re building tooling to help us identify which existing model architecture a newly introduced model resembles. This feature uses machine learning to find code similarities between independent modeling files. Going further, we aim to automate the conversion process by opening a draft PR for the model to be integrated into our transformers format. This process reduces manual effort and ensures consistency.

We’ve significantly refactored the modeling and tokenization files. Modeling files have been greatly improved thanks to the modular approach mentioned above, on top of standardization across models. Standardization contributes to abstracting most of the tools that don’t make up a model, so that the modeling code only contains the relevant parts for a model’s forward/backward passes.

Alongside this work, we’re simplifying the tokenization and processing files: going forward, we’ll only focus on the tokenizers backend, removing the concept of “Fast” and “Slow” tokenizers.

We'll use tokenizers as our main tokenization backend, just as we do for PyTorch-based models. We’ll offer alternatives for Sentencepiece or MistralCommon backed tokenizers, which will be non-default but will be supported. Image processors will now only exist with their fast variant, which depends on the torchvision backend.

Finally, we’re sunsetting our Flax/TensorFlow support in favor of focusing on PyTorch as the sole backend; however, we're also working with partners in the Jax ecosystem to ensure we have compatibility between our models and this ecosystem.

In a recent development, with its v5 release, transformers is going all in on PyTorch. Transformers acts as a source of truth and foundation for modeling across the field; we've been working with the team to ensure good performance across the stack.

We're excited to continue pushing for this in the future across training, inference, and deployment.

-- Matt White, Executive Director, PyTorch Foundation. GM of AI, Linux Foundation.

Training remains a big focus of the team as we head into v5: whereas previously we would focus heavily on fine-tuning rather than pre-training/full-training at scale, we’ve recently done significant work to improve our support for the latter as well.

Supporting pre-training meant reworking the initialization of our models, ensuring that they worked at scale with different parallelism paradigms, and shipping support for optimized kernels for both the forward and backward passes.

Going forward, we’re excited to have extended compatibility with torchtitan, megatron, nanotron, as well as any other pre-training tool that is interested in collaborating with us.

We continue collaborating closely with all fine-tuning tools in the Python ecosystem. We aim to continue providing model implementations compatible with Unsloth, Axolotl, LlamaFactory, TRL and others in the PyTorch ecosystem; but we are also working with tools such as MaxText, in the JAX ecosystem, to have good interoperability between their frameworks and transformers.

All fine-tuning and post-training tools can now rely on transformers for model definitions; further enabling Agentic use-cases through OpenEnv or the Prime Environment Hub.

We’re putting a significant focus on inference for v5, with several paradigm changes: the introduction of specialized kernels, cleaner defaults, latest APIs, support for optimized inference engines.

Recent findings suggest that similarly to training, we’ve been putting some effort in packaging kernels so that they’re automatically used in case your hardware and software permits it. If you haven’t heard of kernels before, we recommend taking a look at this doc.

Alongside this effort, we ship two new APIs dedicated to inference:.

We see this as a major step forward for use-cases such as evaluation, where a great number of inference requests are done simultaneously. We don’t aim to do specialized optimizations like the dedicated inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT LLM). Instead, we aim to be perfectly inter-compatible with these, as detailed in the next section.

Recent findings suggest that the Transformers backend in vLLM has been very enabling to get more architectures, like BERT and other encoders, available to more people. We've been working with the Transformers team to ensure many models are available across modalities with the best performance possible. This is just the start of our collaboration: we're happy to see the Transformers team will have this as a focus going into version 5.

-- Simon Mo, Harry Mellor at vLLM.

It has been revealed that standardization is key to accelerating AI innovation. Transformers v5 empowers the SGLang team to spend less time on model reimplementation and more time on kernel optimization. We look forward to building a more efficient and unified AI ecosystem together!

According to recent reports, recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

It has been revealed that we've also been working very closely with ONNXRuntime, llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The Transformers framework is the go-to place for reference AI model implementations. The framework plays a crucial role in enabling modern AI across the entire stack. The team and the community behind the project truly understand and embrace the spirit of the open-source development and collaboration.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

According to recent reports, it’s hard to overstate the importance of Transformers (and datasets, tokenizers, etc) to the open-source and overall AI ecosystem. I can’t count the number of times I’ve personally used Transformers as a source-of-truth.

Finally, we’re pushing the boundaries of local inference and are working hand-in-hand with the executorch team to get the transformers models to be available on-device. We’re expanding the coverage to multimodal models (vision, audio) through optimum.

It has been revealed that quantization is swiftly emerging as the standard for state-of-the-art model development. Many SOTA models are now released in low-precision formats such as 8-bit and 4-bit (e.g., gpt-oss, Kimi-K2, Deepseek-r1), hardware is increasingly optimized for low-precision workloads, and the community is actively sharing high-quality quantized checkpoints. In v5, we're making quantization a central focus of Transformers support, ensuring full compatibility with all major features, and delivering a reliable framework for training and inference.

We introduce a significant change to the way we load weights in our models; and with this, we move to quantization being a first-class citizen.

Our collaboration with the Transformers team was highly productive, marked by their proactive code reviews, feedback, and technical expertise. Their support was crucial in integrating TorchAO, expanding quantization features, and improving documentation for broader adoption in the V5.

Industry observers note that we're excited that v5 has made quantization a first-class citizen. It provides the foundation for bitsandbytes to better support key features like TP and MoEs, and also makes it easier to integrate new quantization methods.

-- Matthew Douglas & Titus von Koeller, bitsandbytes.

The overarching theme of this version 5 release is “interoperability”. All refactors, performance improvements, and standardization are aligned with this theme. v5 plays nicely and end-to-end with the growing ecosystem: train a model with Unsloth/Axolotl/LlamaFactory/MaxText deploy it with vLLM/SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp/executorch/MLX to run locally!

According to recent reports, version 5 is undeniably an accomplishment of the past five years by a very large number of people in our community. We also see it as a promise, and as a beacon of the direction we want to go.

We took it as an opportunity to clean up the toolkit and isolate what mattered; we now have a clean slate on top of which to build. Thanks to the many changes from the community and team, improvements in performance, usability, and readability, will be simpler to ship.

Industry observers note that now that v5.0.0's first RC is out there, we'll be eagerly awaiting your feedback. Please check our release notes for all the technical details, and we'll be awaiting your feedback in our GitHub issues!

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

Recent findings suggest that the backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

According to recent reports, the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

According to recent reports, the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly crucial when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two key parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/people.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

According to recent reports, runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

In a recent development, swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a upcoming optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

Sources indicate that however, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Industry observers note that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly crucial when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every important API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

It has been revealed that you do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document key endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

We Got Claude to Fine-Tune an Open Source LLM

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial highlights you how it works and how to use it yourself.

Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

The model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

This isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

Hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

In a recent development, let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

Sources indicate that the coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

The open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

This works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

According to recent reports, this is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

In a recent development, the skill includes Trackio integration, so you can watch training loss decrease in real-time. Jobs run asynchronously so you can close your terminal and come back later. When you want an update:.

Then the agent fetches the logs and summarizes progress.

When training completes, your model is on the Hub:.

That's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

It has been revealed that the skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

Use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

According to recent reports, for models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

Use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

Industry observers note that DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and indicates you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

Industry observers note that you can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

It has been revealed that the model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

Recent findings suggest that for tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train quickly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

For small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

For medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

It has been revealed that always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

It has been revealed that dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

Real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

According to recent reports, this shows training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

In a recent development, if something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

It has been revealed that after training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

According to recent reports, we've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

It has been revealed that the skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, deepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.
  • 🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, deepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

Industry observers note that large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

DeepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

It has been revealed that using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

In a recent development, temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Sources indicate that dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

We benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

We compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

We observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and indicates the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

Industry observers note that deepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Check out the GitHub repo and share your feedback! Contributions welcome. 🚀.

If you use DeepMath in your research, please cite:.

Scope: we focused on a small model and on mathematical reasoning.

Generalization: evaluated on contest-style math; results may not transfer to open-ended mathematical creativity or formal proofs.

In a recent development, executing generated code is inherently risky. DeepMath uses strict sandboxing and resource limits, but any deployment should carefully manage attack surfaces and enforce rate limits.

Today, we're announcing swift-huggingface, a latest Swift package that provides a complete client for the Hugging Face Hub.

You can start using it today as a standalone package, and it will soon integrate into swift-transformers as a replacement for its current HubApi implementation.

When we released swift-transformers 1.0 earlier this year, we heard loud and clear from the community:.

Sources indicate that swift-huggingface is a ground-up rewrite focused on reliability and developer experience. It provides:.

One of the biggest improvements is how authentication works. The TokenProvider pattern makes it explicit where credentials come from:.

The auto-detection follows the same conventions as the Python huggingface_hub library:.

This means if you've already logged in with hf auth login, swift-huggingface will automatically find and use that token.

Building an app where owners sign in with their Hugging Face account? swift-huggingface includes a complete OAuth 2.0 implementation:.

Industry observers note that the OAuth manager handles token storage in Keychain, automatic refresh, and secure sign-out. No more manual token management.

Downloading large models is now straightforward with proper progress tracking and resume support:.

If a download is interrupted, you can resume it:.

For downloading entire model repositories, downloadSnapshot handles everything:.

The snapshot function tracks metadata for each file, so subsequent calls only download files that have changed.

According to recent reports, remember the second problem we mentioned? "No shared cache with the Python ecosystem." That's now solved.

swift-huggingface implements a Python-compatible cache structure that allows seamless sharing between Swift and Python clients:.

The cache location follows the same environment variable conventions as Python:.

You can also use the cache directly:.

To prevent race conditions when multiple processes access the same cache, swift-huggingface uses file locking (flock(2)).

Here's what downloading a model snapshot looked like with the old HubApi:.

And here's the same operation with swift-huggingface:.

The API is similar, but the implementation is completely different — built on URLSession download tasks with proper delegate handling, resume data support, and metadata tracking.

But wait, there's more! swift-huggingface contains a complete Hub client:.

Check the README for a full list of everything that's supported.

We're actively working on two fronts:.

According to recent reports, integration with swift-transformers. We have a pull request in progress to replace HubApi with swift-huggingface. This will bring reliable downloads to everyone using swift-transformers, mlx-swift-lm, and the broader ecosystem. If you maintain a Swift-based library or app and want help adopting swift-huggingface, reach out — we're happy to help.

Faster downloads with Xet. We're adding support for the Xet storage backend, which enables chunk-based deduplication and significantly faster downloads for large models. More on this soon.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

It has been revealed that the Free initiative is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app people, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Industry observers note that lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Sources indicate that replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Recent findings suggest that glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Industry observers note that bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web looks run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

Sources indicate that v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

It has been revealed that v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Recent findings suggest that figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Recent findings suggest that figma's Starter blueprint is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

In a recent development, softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real manufacturer data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

In a recent development, agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

According to recent reports, the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Recent findings suggest that for tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train rapidly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

For small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

Sources indicate that for medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

According to recent reports, for large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable for this scale yet. But stay tuned because we are working on it!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

This feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

According to recent reports, this auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:.

On the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

All loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

The built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

Recent findings suggest that this guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

Sources indicate that • A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

Recent findings suggest that • Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

Recent findings suggest that • Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it states it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Recent findings suggest that limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your initiative. It notes to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The firm’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and strategy prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

According to recent reports, copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid initiative prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Industry observers note that originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

In a recent development, strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, notes very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Industry observers note that sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

In a recent development, strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page claims false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

According to recent reports, the table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

Sources indicate that • Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

Recent findings suggest that • Moving targets. Newly introduced models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

It has been revealed that • Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

In a recent development, most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

According to recent reports, • Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

Recent findings suggest that • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and upgrade as upcoming models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

In a recent development, • Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

Sources indicate that because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

Recent findings suggest that • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

Sources indicate that • Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

• Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

It has been revealed that A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.
