📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA today released Cosmos Reason 2, the latest advancement in open, reasoning vision language models for physical AI. Cosmos Reason 2 surpasses its previous version in accuracy and tops the Physical AI Bench and Physical Reasoning leaderboards as the #1 open model for visual understanding.

It has been revealed that since their introduction, vision-language models have rapidly improved at tasks like object and pattern recognition in images. But they still struggle with tasks humans find natural, like planning several steps ahead, dealing with uncertainty or adapting to new situations. Cosmos Reason is designed to close this gap by giving robots and AI agents stronger common sense and reasoning to solve complex problems step by step.

Sources indicate that cosmos Reason 2 is a state-of-the-art, open reasoning vision-language model (VLM) that enables robots and AI agents to see, understand, blueprint, and act in the physical world like humans. It uses common sense, physics, and prior knowledge to recognize how objects move across space and time to handle complex tasks, adapt to new situations, and figure out how to solve problems step by step.

Improved spatio-temporal understanding and timestamp precision.

Optimized performance with flexible deployment options from edge to cloud with 2B and 8B parameters model sizes.

Support for expanded set of spatial understanding and visual perception capabilities — 2D/3D point localization, bounding box coordinates, trajectory data, and OCR support.

Improved long-context understanding with 256K input tokens, up from 16K with Cosmos Reason 1.

Adaptable to multiple use cases with easy-to-use Cosmos Cookbook recipes.

Video analytics AI agents — These agents can extract valuable insights from massive volumes of video data to optimize processes. Cosmos Reason 2 builds on the capabilities of Cosmos Reason 1 and now provides OCR support, as well as 2D/3D point localization and a set of mark understanding.

Developers can jumpstart development of video analytics AI agents by using the NVIDIA blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Salesforce is transforming workplace safety and compliance by analyzing video footage captured by Cobalt robots with Agentforce and VSS blueprint with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Data annotation and critique — Enable developers to automate high-quality annotation and critique of massive, diverse training datasets. Cosmos Reason provides time stamps and detailed descriptions for real or synthetically generated training videos.

It has been revealed that uber is exploring Cosmos Reason 2 to deliver accurate, searchable video captions for autonomous vehicle (AV) training data, enabling efficient identification of critical driving scenarios. This co-authored Reason 2 for AV Video Captioning and VQA recipe demonstrates how to fine-tune and evaluate Cosmos Reason 2-8B on annotated AV videos. Across multiple evaluation metrics, measurable improvements were achieved: BLEU scores improved 10.6% (0.113 → 0.125), MCQ-based VQA gained 0.67 percentage points (80.18% → 80.85%), and LingoQA increased 13.8% (63.2% → 77.0%). These gains demonstrate effective domain adaptation for AV applications.

Sources indicate that robot planning and reasoning — Act as the brain for deliberate, methodical decision-making in a robot vision language action (VLA) model. Cosmos Reason 2 now provides trajectory coordinates in addition to determining next steps.

Encord provides native support for Cosmos Reason 2 in its Data Agent library and AI data platform, enabling developers to leverage Cosmos Reason 2 as a VLA for robotics and other physical AI use cases.

Companies like Hitachi, Milestone and VAST Data are using Cosmos Reason to advance robotics, autonomous driving, and video analytics AI agents for traffic and workplace safety.

According to recent reports, try Cosmos Reason 2 on build.nvidia.com and experience the latest features with sample prompts for generating bounding boxes and robot trajectories. Upload your own videos and images for further analysis.

Download Cosmos Reason 2 models (2B and 8B) on Hugging Face or use Cosmos Reason 2 in the cloud. The model will be available soon on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. To get started, check out Cosmos Reason 2 documentation and the Cosmos Cookbook.

Cosmos Predict is a generative AI model that predicts future states of the physical world as video, based on text, image, or video inputs.

Cosmos Transfer is our lightest multicontrol model built for video to world style transfer.

NVIDIA GR00T N1.6 is an open reasoning vision language action (VLA) model, purpose-built for humanoid robots, that unlocks full body control and uses NVIDIA Cosmos Reason for better reasoning and contextual understanding.

#126619. I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1300 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance.
  • Sources indicate that developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal.
  • It has been revealed that the first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance. Voyaging uncharted waters may appear foolish to some, yet folly and heroism can often appear the same to the undiscerning eye," so notes the voice of Johannes Zuch - creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' behind Leonida's latest favourite indie darling art game, Tenebrae Lux. It's pretentious, it's deeply up its own arse, and it's awkward and off-putting to play. A must-review for Eurogamer.

Sources indicate that developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal. Jason is quick to dismiss Tenebrae Lux in company, but once Cal slinks off home - hungover and dreary - I slide the disc back into my JoyStation console and sink my teeth back into it. Jason loves this stuff, really. He only keeps Time Jackers: Rewind installed so his mates don't judge him.

It has been revealed that the first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name. It's Latin for 'darkness and light', or something similar. Is this riffing on Clair Obscur, which is French for 'light dark'? No, it's too cerebral for that - too plodding and navel-gazey. Sandfall Interactive wouldn't be this pretentious. Maybe it's a pastiche of Dear Esther, then, drawing on the tenets and schema of the 'walking simulator' genre and using that washed-out film noir aesthetic. But then, it's too wordy for that, with too many interactive and puzzle-adjacent elements. Ah, it must be mocking The Witness, instead - there's the telltale lighthouse, the 'I'm definitely not telling you where to go and what to do' internal narration, and of course the fingerprints of Johannes Zuch are all over it. Johannes Zuch, Jonathan Blow - see how they braided them together? (Sorry).

It has been revealed that whilst this has been created by Rockstar as a pastiche - as much loving send-up as it is withering take down - and designed to make a quick joke in the early 'Feng Shui' mission, the game is playable from start to finish if you so desire. You boot it up by inserting a physical disc, too, which is funny given the context. And it's good! Well, not good good, but it's a proper brainteaser, and ribs 2016's The Witness with such knowledge and (I think?) respect that it's hard not to be charmed by Rockstar's game-within-a-game. There are collectibles to be found that riff on Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves, too, a knowing nod to the most try-hard of all try-hard literature.

According to recent reports, within seconds of the title screen, too, you're presented with a game-within-a-game-within-a-game. You must clear four boards filled with puzzle pieces as the protagonist mutters something mysterious and weird in his posh voice. Do so, and you unlock the door to the next location. Head up to a bunker, and you'll see a room filled with various clues - maybe it's a flashing lamp flickering in morse code, maybe it's a malfunctioning clock presenting a maths puzzle, maybe it's a pricetag on a record that changes on every visit, maybe it's a photograph with anomalous elements, maybe it's a "Developed Using Zuchworks Engine" easter egg hidden in the environment. You need to keep your wits about you, because one of these clues changes every time you enter - and the clue corresponds to a date that changes on a calendar on the wall.

You can look up a guide if you need to, or you can spend far too long figuring out how all this relates to the telephone you can find in the room on your own, like muggins here, before opening up the path to the next puzzle. Look at the image below to see the level of record-keeping and brainteasing this bizarre little game prompted from me. I will say, the sense of achievement you get from playing around with this stuff is pretty remarkable, given - let's not forget I'm actually playing Grand Theft Auto 6 whilst I'm wandering around in the black and white murk trying to complete a puzzle game for no actual reward.

Industry observers note that the bunker room is, by far, the hardest part of Tenebrae Lux. From here, things ease up: you need to figure out the right sequence of glyphs on a bridge, and then put some distance between yourself and a curious and rather creepy suited man that's seemingly figuring things out ahead of you in a location inspired by, I think, The Backrooms (or Portal, or Superliminal, or maybe something else entirely. Who knows what Zuch was thinking?).

"With the last enigma finally mastered," the narrator drones in his bumbling monotone, "I step forward into the void, the shadows swallow, consuming all, and then finally the sweet embrace of darkness of which there is no end." 'You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience', Tenebrae Lux tells me, before cutting to the best joke of the whole thing: the credits roll much akin to something Hideo Kojima would produce.

So, what do you get out of all of this? Well - just like real puzzle games in the real world - nothing, really. If you've not completed one of the other three fully playable games in GTA 6, you will get a trophy/achievement. But given the main game is all about Jason and Lucia's desperate scramble to escape the poverty trap, to try and break free of the cycle of debt, violence, and consequence that keeps them clinging to Leonida's seedy underbelly, there's no monetary reward. There's no 'progress' in the sense of the protagonist's shared story.

Sources indicate that even in terms of your own cold, hard, mathematical 'completion' you only need to boot each of the four games up once in order to work towards GTA 6's 100% completion. So what's the point of all this? Why did I spend the better part of 90 minutes trying to figure out how to find a sliver of light in the dark in Tenebrae Lux? The game is a wonderful pastiche in that, essentially, it's not really saying anything. You can probably project some vague meaning onto it if you wish - I'm pretty certain the protagonist literally 'finds himself' at the end - but glib little readings like that are ten-a-penny in this genre.

I think the most impressive thing about Tenebrae Lux is that it exists. You're teased with it in an early mission - Rockstar may as well say 'look, we put a game in a game, lol' - but it's more than that. This is what happens when Rockstar's 4700-plus developers are given the room to… develop. Tenebrae Lux could very easily have been a non-interactive experience, a quick, cheap joke shown over-the-shoulder taking a drive-by pop shot at Johnathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck, or any and all of the above. Or maybe it could be a 'vertical slice', an incomplete demo, a teaser. But it's not, because nothing about GTA 6 is quick or cheap.

According to recent reports, GTA 6, in every single conceivable way, is a premium experience - part-sandbox, part-simulation, part-otherworld. To create not just one, but four fully playable and completable games within that framework is showboating, sure, but to make that game actually good and - perhaps controversially - even better than some of the games it's pastiching… Well, it's just rubbing salt in the wound, really.

A code for the game was provided by Cal Hampton.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the newly introduced game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

Recent findings suggest that right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

It has been revealed that called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Industry observers note that hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their new life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

In a recent development, until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

"Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community.".

Recent findings suggest that here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

It's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It highlights us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

According to recent reports, it may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Open Responses is a fresh and open inference standard.
  • The era of the chatbot is long gone, and agents dominate inference workloads.
  • According to recent reports, this mismatch between the agentic workflow requirements and entrenched interfaces motivates the need for an open inference standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open Responses is a fresh and open inference standard. Initiated by OpenAI, built by the open source AI community, and backed by the Hugging Face ecosystem, Open Responses is based on the Responses API and is designed for the future of Agents. In this blog post, we’ll look at how Open Responses works and why the open source community should use Open Responses.

The era of the chatbot is long gone, and agents dominate inference workloads. Developers are shifting toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act over long-time horizons. Despite this shift, much of the ecosystem still uses the Chat Completion format, which was designed for turn-based conversations and falls short for agentic use cases. The Responses format was designed to address these limitations, but it is closed and not as widely adopted. The Chat Completion format is still the de facto standard despite the alternatives.

According to recent reports, this mismatch between the agentic workflow requirements and entrenched interfaces motivates the need for an open inference standard. Over the coming months, we will collaborate with the community and inference providers to implement and adapt Open Responses to a shared format, practically capable of replacing chat completions.

Open Responses builds on the direction OpenAI has set with their Responses API introduced in March 2025, which superseded the existing Completion and Assistants APIs with a consistent way to:.

Open Responses extends and open-sources the Responses API, making it more accessible for builders and routing providers to interoperate and collaborate on shared interests.

We’ll briefly explore the core changes that impact most community members. If you want to deep dive into the specification, check out the Open Responses documentation.

Client requests to Open Responses are similar to the existing Responses API. Below we demonstrate a request to the Open Responses API using curl. We're calling a proxy endpoint that routes to Inference Providers using the Open Responses API schema.

Industry observers note that clients that already support the Responses API can migrate to Open Responses with relatively little effort. The main changes involve how reasoning content is exposed:.

OpenAI models used to only expose summary and encrypted_content. With Open Responses, providers may expose their raw reasoning via the API. Clients migrating from providers that previously returned only summaries and encrypted content will now have the opportunity to receive and handle raw reasoning streams when supported by their chosen provider.

For Model Providers, implementing the changes for Open Responses should be straightforward if they already adhere to the Responses API specification. For Routers, there is now the opportunity to standardize on a consistent endpoint and support configuration options for customization where needed.

Over time, as Providers continue to innovate, certain features will become standardized in the base specification.

In summary, migrating to Open Responses will make the inference experience more consistent and improve quality as undocumented extensions, interpretations, and workarounds of the legacy Completions API are normalized in Open Responses.

You can see how to stream reasoning chunks below.

Here’s the difference between getting an Open Response and using OpenAI Responses for reasoning deltas:.

Open Responses distinguishes between “Model Providers” — those who provide inference — and “Routers” — intermediaries who orchestrate between multiple providers.

Clients can now specify a Provider along with provider-specific API options when making requests, allowing intermediary Routers to orchestrate requests between upstream providers.

Open Responses natively supports two categories of tools: internal and external. Externally hosted tools are implemented outside the model provider’s system. For example, client side functions to be executed, or MCP servers. Internally hosted tools are within the model provider’s system. For example, OpenAI’s file search or Google Drive integration. The model calls, executes, and retrieves results entirely within the provider's infrastructure, requiring no developer intervention.

Open Responses formalizes the agentic loop which is usually made up of a repeating cycle of reasoning, tool invocation, and response generation that enables models to autonomously complete multi-step tasks.

image source: openresponses.org.

For internally-hosted tools, the provider manages the entire loop; executing tools, returning results to the model, and streaming output. This means that multi-step workflows like "search documents, summarize findings, then draft an email" use a single request.

Clients control loop behavior via max_tool_calls to cap iterations and tool_choice to constrain which tools are invocable:.

The response contains all intermediate items: tool calls, results, reasoning.

Open Responses extends and improves the Responses API, providing richer and more detailed content definitions, compatibility, and deployment options. It also provides a standard way to execute sub-agent loops during primary inference calls, opening up powerful capabilities for AI Applications. We are looking forward to working with the Open Responses team and the community at large on future development of the specification.

You can try Open Responses with Hugging Face Inference Providers today. We have an early access version available for use on Hugging Face Spaces - try it with your Client and Open Responses Compliance Tool today!

AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • In a recent development, the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • Recent findings suggest that published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

In a recent development, the team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Recent findings suggest that published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

Sources indicate that "Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

According to recent reports, visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

In a recent development, the fresh findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

Sources indicate that an notable opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

According to recent reports, at Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

In a recent development, producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

According to recent reports, to address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another crucial discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

Sources indicate that the findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

According to recent reports, the participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

Industry observers note that the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring owners to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

Industry observers note that "A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

Recent findings suggest that the research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

Sources indicate that the project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, waypoint-1 is Overworld’s real-time-interactive video diffusion model, controllable and prompted via text, mouse, and keyboard.
  • The backbone of the model is a frame-causal rectified flow transformer trained on 10,000 hours of diverse video game footage paired with control inputs and text captions.
  • The standard among existing world models has become taking pre-trained video models and fine-tuning them with brief and simplified control inputs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Overworld Stream: https://overworld.stream.

According to recent reports, waypoint-1 is Overworld’s real-time-interactive video diffusion model, controllable and prompted via text, mouse, and keyboard. You can give the model some frames, run the model, and have it create a world you can step into and interact with.

The backbone of the model is a frame-causal rectified flow transformer trained on 10,000 hours of diverse video game footage paired with control inputs and text captions. Waypoint-1 is a latent model, meaning that it is trained on compressed frames.

The standard among existing world models has become taking pre-trained video models and fine-tuning them with brief and simplified control inputs. In contrast, Waypoint-1 is trained from the get-go with a focus on interactive experiences. With other models, controls are simple: you can move and rotate the camera once every few frames, with severe latency issues. With Waypoint-1 you are not limited at all as far as controls are concerned. You can move the camera freely with the mouse, and input any key on the keyboard, and all this with zero latency. Each frame is generated with your controls as context. Additionally, the model runs fast enough to provide a seamless experience even on consumer hardware.

In a recent development, waypoint-1 was pre-trained via diffusion forcing, a technique with which the model learns to denoise future frames given past frames. A causal attention mask is applied such that a token in any given frame can only attend to tokens in its own frame, or past frames, but not future frames. Each frame is noised randomly, and as such the model learns to denoise each frame separately. During inference, you can then denoise new frames one at a time, allowing you to generate a procedural stream of new frames.

While diffusion forcing presents a strong baseline, randomly noising all frames is misaligned with a frame-by-frame autoregressive rollout. This inference mismatch results in error accumulation, and noisy long rollouts. To address this problem we post-train with self forcing, a technique that trains the model to produce realistic outputs under a regime which matches inference behavior. Self-forcing via DMD has the added benefit of one-pass CFG, and few-step denoising.

According to recent reports, worldEngine is Overworld’s high‑performance inference library for interactive world model streaming. It provides the core tooling for building inference applications in pure Python, optimized for low latency, high throughput, extensibility, and developer simplicity. The runtime loop is designed for interactivity: it consumes context frame images, keyboard/mouse inputs, and text, and outputs image frames for real‑time streaming.

On Waypoint‑1‑Small (2.3B) running on a 5090, WorldEngine sustains ~30,000 token‑passes/sec (single denoising pass; 256 tokens per frame) and achieves 30 FPS at 4 steps or 60 FPS at 2 steps.

Performance comes from four targeted optimizations:.

We’d love to see what you can come up with to extend the world_engine and it should be a great event to meet like-minded founders, engineers, hackers and investors. Running an AI agent on your own GPU sounds simple: point it at Ollama and stop paying per token. I set up OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant, with a 9B model in Ollama on one RTX 3090 and connected it to Discord. Then I read the Ollama log for every request.

The agent worked. The numbers were not what I expected, though. A one-line question turned into a prompt of more than 18,000 tokens, the first reply took over a minute, and the small model sometimes guessed instead of using its tools.

This article covers what I measured and what each number means if you initiative to run an agent on local hardware.

In a recent development, openClaw ran in Docker and reached Ollama on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434. Discord was the chat interface, and OpenClaw's web panel highlighted the sessions and context use.

This article is about the results, not the installation. The full step-by-step setup is in a separate guide to running OpenClaw in Docker with Ollama and Discord. That guide covers the Compose file, the Discord bot and how to keep the ports off your network.

It has been revealed that all timings below come from the Ollama log on the test machine. Ollama loaded the model with a 32,768-token context.

My first message in Discord was short: "Which model are you running on, and what is 17 * 23?" The bot answered correctly: it ran on ollama/qwen3.5:9b, and 17 × 23 is 391.

In a recent development, the Ollama log highlighted what that question cost. The model processed 18,415 prompt tokens and generated 33 tokens.

Industry observers note that the extra tokens come from the agent itself. With every request, OpenClaw sends:.

Industry observers note that on the RTX 3090, reading that prompt took 10 seconds at 1,838 tokens per second. A slower GPU, or a CPU, needs much longer to read the same prompt.

In a recent development, prompt tokens per model call, from the Ollama log. Only the first message had to process the whole prompt.

OpenClaw counts tokens with its own estimate, which was higher than the Ollama count. The gateway log estimated the prompt at 24,608 tokens, against a prompt budget of 24,576 tokens for this model. By OpenClaw's own count, the base prompt alone used up the budget before any conversation history.

The web panel demonstrated a similar figure: 68 to 69 percent of the context window was in use for the Discord sessions after only a few messages.

The first message arrived while the model was not loaded in GPU memory. That reply took 1 min 10 s:.

The next requests were much faster:.

Reply times on the test machine. Loading the model took most of the first reply.

It has been revealed that the speed-up comes from prompt caching. The system prompt, tool definitions and workspace files at the start of the prompt stay the same between requests. Ollama kept that part cached and processed only the new tokens. The model wrote at 91 to 96 tokens per second in every test.

In a recent development, ollama's documentation notes models stay in memory for 5 minutes by default before they are unloaded. After that, the next message pays the load time again. You can change this with the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE environment variable on the Ollama server, or with the keep_alive parameter per request. A negative value, such as -1, keeps the model loaded. I did not change this setting in the test.

If you run Ollama in Docker, pass the variable with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1 or in the environment: section of your Compose file.

Two things used the GPU besides my chat messages.

A heartbeat. OpenClaw's web panel listed one scheduled automation, heartbeat-main, which runs every 30 minutes. The agent wakes on that schedule, so the model gets called even when nobody chats. With Ollama's 5-minute default, the model is unloaded between heartbeats unless someone chatted recently, so a heartbeat most likely starts with a model load. I did not measure this.

An embedding model. During the first message, OpenClaw also called Ollama's /api/embed endpoint twice to index its memory. It used qwen3-embedding:4b, which was already installed on the Ollama server. I did not set OpenClaw to use that model; it picked it on its own.

The two models took this much GPU memory:.

That is 11.4 GB for the models alone, almost half of the RTX 3090's 24 GB.

The rest of the stack was light:.

Sources indicate that what this means for you: plan GPU memory for the chat model, the embedding model and the context, not the chat model alone. If the GPU also runs other models, the heartbeat can compete with them.

The first two tests in Discord: a question, then a file written with a tool. The user name is blurred.

The mistakes showed up when the model had to check something:.

After the restart, the bot claimed it had lost the earlier session. When asked to use its read tool, it read the file correctly.

In a recent development, the fix for the first problem was simple. When I wrote "use your read tool to open homelab-test.md", the model opened the file and listed all three points correctly. Naming the tool made it check instead of guess.

The model listed four files and missed the test file and a folder, because it answered from its prompt.

Based on this test, a local 9B model on one consumer GPU works for:.

If you need better answers, OpenClaw also works with hosted models, but then your prompts leave your machine.

According to recent reports, in this test, qwen3.5:9b used 6.3 GB and the qwen3-embedding:4b memory model used 5.1 GB. Together the two models needed 11.4 GB.

Sources indicate that the model had to load into GPU memory first, which took 59 seconds of the 70-second reply. Ollama keeps a model loaded for 5 minutes by default, and the OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE setting changes that.

Every request includes OpenClaw's system prompt, its tool definitions and its workspace files. A one-line question became an 18,415-token prompt in this test.

Industry observers note that yes. A heartbeat automation runs every 30 minutes and calls the model even when nobody sends a message.

Sources indicate that it handled questions, arithmetic and file creation correctly in this test. It sometimes answered from its prompt instead of using its tools. When it wrongly mentioned its memory was lost, asking it to use its read tool made it check the file and answer correctly.

#126613. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

In a recent development, using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

In a recent development, another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially notable.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Industry observers note that because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

It has been revealed that "One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

Sources indicate that doctors presently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

According to recent reports, the approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

Recent findings suggest that "In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer stated. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

Industry observers note that the researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

It has been revealed that "Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a massive part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Industry observers note that obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal Fresh Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most notable contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

Note DIFF V2 subtracts two heads that are in the same GQA group, which means they share the same key and value. This is crucial to performance. See design ablations section and Github code.

The λ\lambdaλ in DIFF V2 is projected from XXX for each token each head.

DIFF V2 doubles number of query heads while maintaining number of key value heads, and the extra dimension is reduced back to h*d after the differential operation so the WOW_OWO​ projection remains the same as baseline Transformer.

Industry observers note that DIFF V2 introduces additional query heads compared to the baseline Transformer, but does not increase the number of key-value (KV) heads. Since LLM decoding is typically memory-bound, this design allows DIFF V2 to achieve decoding speeds on par with standard Transformer. Besides, since head dimension is aligned between query, key and value, there is no need for custom attention kernels for DIFF V2. In contrast, DIFF V1 can be slower during decoding because the value cache must be loaded twice, and a custom attention kernel is needed. DIFF V2 can also increase the arithmetic intensity of the attention module during decoding.

Industry observers note that during pretraining, when using cutting-edge FlashAttention kernels on H-series and B-series GPUs, the throughput reduction introduced by DIFF V2 is negligible. For long-sequence prefilling, we recommend combining DIFF V2 with techniques such as YOCO (also used in Gemma 3n), which already reduces prefilling complexity to linear time with respect to sequence length.

An alternative perspective is to compare DIFF V2 with a Transformer that has the same query dimension 2h*d. Under this comparison, both models exhibit same attention kernel speed, while DIFF V2 has less parameters and flops in output projection.

This means the RMSNorm layer applies a 100x magnification to the output. In large-scale pretraining, we find this leads to massive gradients and numerical instability.

A typical phenomenon is that when DIFF V1 is pre-trained at a large learning rate, the gradient norm experiences a larger increase compared to Transformer in the later stages, along with higher variance. In DIFF V2, after removing the per-head RMSNorm, the gradient norm scale becomes comparable to that of Transformer, and the gradient norm spike is reduced (will be discussed further below).

We adopted the per-head RMSNorm design in DIFF V1 primarily because of the doubled value head dimension and the globally shared λ\lambdaλ across all tokens. Given the modifications made to these two aspects in DIFF V2, we found that removing RMSNorm is now safe.

In theory, a standard Transformer with 2h2h2h attention heads can learn the differential operation by learning WO2i=−WO2i+1,i=0,1,…,h−1W_O^{2i}=-W_O^{2i+1}, i=0,1,\ldots,h-1WO2i​=−WO2i+1​,i=0,1,…,h−1, where WOiW_O^{i}WOi​ denotes the output projection of head iii, and head 2i2i2i and 2i+12i+12i+1 belong to the same GQA group.

In a recent development, assumption 1. In practice, such a solution is difficult to learn through optimization, as it requires two sets of parameters to converge to exact negatives of each other.

Assumption 2. The differential operation can be learned by the model and the model chooses to learn it in the training. Then explicitly constructing it before the output projection as in DIFF V2 can save half of the WOW_OWO​ parameters. The number of saved parameters is also non-trivial. Under the current GQA setting, the parameters in the attention module are dominated by WQW_QWQ​ and WOW_OWO​; Therefore, approximately 25% of the attention-module parameters can be saved. The saved parameter budget can then be reallocated to other parts of the model.

Even if DIFF V2, after reallocating parameters, does not achieve a lower loss than the baseline but merely matches it, the method is still worthwhile if it provides additional benefits such as improved training stability, better control of outliers, or higher training efficiency. This is analogous to GQA, which matches the loss of MHA while reducing KV-cache as an additional benefit. So the key question becomes empirical performance.

In a recent development, (For simplicity, we omit the batch dimension and assume that both the input and output of the following flash_attn_func are three-dimensional tensors (tokens, heads, head dimension). Heads belonging to the same GQA group are arranged contiguously in the output).

Industry observers note that in our large learning rate setting, the ablation 1 setting exhibits obvious training instability (much more loss and gradient spikes) and higher loss comparing to DIFF V2. The value should be shared in the two subtraction heads to construct differential operation, as discussed in DIFF V1 paper.

According to recent reports, both ablation 2 and ablation 3 lead to higher language modeling loss than DIFF V2. Ablation 2 maintains training stability similar to DIFF V2, whereas ablation 3 is less stable (still more stable than ablation 1).

Ablation 4 also has higher training loss comparing to DIFF V2.

It has been revealed that this is a fascinating and thorough patch on the Differential Transformer architecture. The transition from DIFF V1 to V2 addresses some critical practical hurdles in a very elegant way.

The key design choice of doubling query heads within shared GQA groups is clever. It successfully decouples the innovative "differential" attention operation from the need for custom kernels, making it a much more viable drop-in replacement for standard attention. The analysis of how this design overcomes the softmax magnitude constraint and helps eliminate attention sinks is particularly convincing.

Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • According to recent reports, the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising latest method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

According to recent reports, the technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Latest Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

Recent findings suggest that quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can swiftly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

It has been revealed that but quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," notes Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

It has been revealed that rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify crucial interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

It has been revealed that "From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, indicated that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an key step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

It has been revealed that "This is particularly vital because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

It has been revealed that looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

Industry observers note that "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.

Sources indicate that this shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how rapidly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

Industry observers note that the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the first blog addresses strategic changes and the explosion of upcoming open models and open source players. The second covers architectural and hardware choices largely by Chinese companies made in the wake of a growing open ecosystem, available here. The third analyzes prominent organizations’ trajectories and the future of the global open source ecosystem, available here.

Sources indicate that for AI researchers and developers contributing to and relying on the open source ecosystem and for policymakers understanding the rapidly changing environment, there has never been a better time to build and release open models and artifacts, as proven by the past year’s immense growth catalyzed by DeepSeek. Notably, geopolitics has driven adoption; while models developed in China have been dominating across metrics throughout 2025 and newly introduced players leapfrogging each other, Western AI communities are seeking commercially deployable alternatives.

Before R1, China’s AI industry was still largely centered on closed models. Open models had existed for years, but they were mostly confined to research communities or used only in niche scenarios such as privacy-sensitive applications. For most companies, they were not the default choice. Compute resources were tight, and whether to “open or close” was a subject of debate.

It has been revealed that deepSeek’s R1 model lowered the barrier to advanced AI capabilities and offered a clear pattern to follow, unlocking a second layer. Moreover, the release gave Chinese AI development something extremely valuable: time. It demonstrated that even with limited resources, rapid progress was still possible through open source and fast iteration. This approach aligned naturally with the goals set out in China’s 2017 “AI+” strategy: combining AI with industry as early as possible, while continuing to build up compute capacity over the long term.

One year after the release of R1, what we see emerging is not only a collection of new models, but also a growing organic open source AI ecosystem.

According to recent reports, for the first time, an open model from China entered the global mainstream rankings and, over the following year, was repeatedly used as a reference point when upcoming models were released. DeepSeek’s R1 swiftly became the most liked model on Hugging Face of all time and the top liked models are no longer majority U.S.-developed.

But R1’s real significance was not whether it was the strongest model at the time, its importance lay in how it lowered three barriers.

Industry observers note that the first was the technical barrier. By openly sharing its reasoning paths and post-training methods, R1 turned advanced reasoning, previously locked behind closed APIs, into an engineering asset that could be downloaded, distilled, and fine-tuned. Many teams no longer needed to train massive models from scratch to gain strong reasoning capabilities. Reasoning started to behave like a reusable module, applied again and again across different systems. This also pushed the industry to rethink the relationship between model capability and compute cost, a shift that was especially meaningful in a compute-constrained environment like China.

It has been revealed that the second was the adoption barrier. R1 was released under the MIT license, making its use, modification, and redistribution straightforward. Companies that had relied on closed models began bringing R1 directly into production. Distillation, secondary training, and domain-specific adaptation became routine engineering work rather than special projects. As distribution constraints fell away, the model quickly spread into cloud platforms and toolchains, and community discussions shifted from “which model scores higher” to “how do we deploy it, reduce cost, and integrate it into real systems.” Over time, R1 moved beyond being a research artifact and became a reusable engineering foundation.

In a recent development, the third change was psychological. When the question shifted from “can we do this?” to “how do we do this well?”, decision-making across many companies changed. For the Chinese AI community, this was also a rare moment of sustained global attention, one that mattered deeply to an ecosystem long seen mainly as a follower.

Together, the lowering of these three barriers meant that the ecosystem began to gain the ability to replicate itself.

Once open source moved into the mainstream, a natural question followed: how would Chinese companies' strategies change?Over the past year, the answer became clear: competition began to shift from model-to-model comparisons toward system level capabilities.

Compared with 2024, the period after the release of R1 saw China’s AI landscape settle into a new pattern. Large technology companies took the lead, startups followed quickly, and companies from vertical industries increasingly entered the field. While their paths differed, a shared understanding gradually emerged, especially among leading players: open source was no longer a short-term tactic, but part of long-term competitive strategy.

Recent findings suggest that the number of competitive Chinese organizations releasing state of the art models and repositories skyrocketed. Reflected in Hugging Face Repository Growth of Chinese Companies, the number of open releases from existing giants substantially increased, with Baidu going from zero releases on Hugging Face in 2024 to over 100 in 2025, and others such as ByteDance and Tencent increasing releases by eight to nine times. An influx of newly open organizations released highly performant models, with Moonshot’s open release, Kimi K2, being a “another DeepSeek moment”.

Releases became stronger and frequent, with performant models released on a weekly basis; newly created Chinese models consistently became most liked and downloaded every week, boasting highest popularity among the top most downloaded newly introduced models on Hugging Face. The Top Newly Created Models by Week on Hugging Face highlights new repositories labeled by organization location or base model organization location for popular derivatives.

As seen in Hugging Face’s heatmap data, between February and July 2025, open releases from Chinese companies became noticeably more active. Baidu and Moonshot moved from primarily closed approaches toward open release. Zhipu AI’s GLM and Alibaba’s Qwen went a step further, expanding from simply publishing model weights to building engineering systems and ecosystem interfaces. At this stage, comparing raw model performance alone was no longer enough to win. Competition increasingly centered on ecosystems, application scenarios, and infrastructure_._.

This strategy was effectively successful; of newly created models (<1 year), downloads for Chinese models have surpassed any other country including the U.S.

According to recent reports, chinese AI players are not coordinating by agreement, but by constraint. What looks like collaboration is better understood as alignment under shared technical, economic, and regulatory pressures. This does not mean companies formed cooperative alliances. Rather, under similar constraints around compute, cost, and compliance, they began competing along similar technical foundations and engineering paths. When competition takes place on comparable system structures, the ecosystem starts to show the ability to spread and grow on its own. Tech leaders from Zhipu AI (Z.ai), Moonshot AI, Alibaba’s Qwen, and Tencent coordinating on shared questions is rarely seen in other countries.

Positive sentiment toward open source adoption and development has increased worldwide and especially in the U.S., with broader recognition of how open source leadership is critical in global competitiveness.

In a recent development, deepSeek has been heavily adopted in global markets, especially in Southeast Asia and Africa. In these markets, factors such as multilingual support, open-weight availability, and cost considerations have supported enterprise use.

Industry observers note that often Western organizations seek non-Chinese models for commercial deployment. Major releases from U.S. organizations such as OpenAI’s gpt-oss, AI2’s Olmo, and Meta’s Llama 4 received community engagement. Reflection AI announced its efforts to build frontier American open-weight models. In France, Mistral released their Mistral Large 3 family, continuously developing their open source roots.

It has been revealed that at the same time, major releases in the West build on Chinese models; in November 2025, Deep Cogito released Cogito v2.1 as the leading U.S. open-weight model. The model was a fine-tuned version of DeepSeek-V3. Startups and researchers globally using open-weight models are often defaulting to if not relying on models developed in China.

In a recent development, the American Truly Open Model (ATOM) project cites DeepSeek and China’s model momentum as a motivator for concerted efforts toward leading in open-weight model development. The project emphasizes the need for multiple efforts and its research also highlights OpenAI’s gpt-oss heavy early adoption.

In a recent development, the world is still responding, with a fresh open source fervor. 2026 is shaping up for major releases , especially from China and the U.S. Of high relevance are the architectural trends, hardware choices, and organizational directions, which will be covered next in this series.
