Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Recent findings suggest that shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that strategy. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

In a recent development, whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide reveals how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

Industry observers note that wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and aims auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the tech giant states you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Industry observers note that saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

It has been revealed that own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AssetOpsBench is a comprehensive benchmark and evaluation system with six qualitative dimensions that bridges the gap for agentic AI in domain-specific settings, starting with industrial Asset Lifecycle Management.

Recent findings suggest that while existing AI benchmarks excel at isolated tasks such as coding or web navigation, they often fail to capture the complexity of real-world industrial operations. To bridge this gap, we introduce AssetOpsBench, a framework specifically designed to evaluate agent performance across six critical dimensions of industrial applications. Unlike traditional benchmarks, AssetOpsBench emphasizes the need for multi-agent coordination—moving beyond `lone wolf' models to systems that can handle complex failure modes, integrate multiple data streams, and manage intricate work orders. By focusing on these high-stakes, multi-agent dynamics, the benchmark ensures that AI agents are assessed on their ability to navigate the nuances and safety-critical demands of a true industrial environment.

AssetOpsBench is built for asset operations such as chillers and air handling units. It comprises:.

According to recent reports, experts helped curate 150+ scenarios. Each scenario includes metadata: task type, output format, category, and sub-agents. The tasks designed span across:.

Recent findings suggest that assetOpsBench evaluates agentic systems across six qualitative dimensions designed to reflect real operational constraints in industrial asset management. Rather than optimizing for a single success metric, the benchmark emphasizes decision trace quality, evidence grounding, failure awareness, and actionability under incomplete and noisy data.

Each agent run is scored across six criteria:.

In a recent development, across early evaluations, we observe that many general-purpose agents perform well on surface-level reasoning but struggle with sustained multi-step coordination involving work orders, failure semantics, and temporal dependencies. Agents that explicitly model operational context and uncertainty tend to produce more stable and interpretable trajectories, even when final task completion is partial.

This feedback-oriented evaluation is intentional: in industrial settings, understanding why an agent fails is often more valuable than a binary success signal.

It has been revealed that A central contribution of AssetOpsBench is the explicit treatment of failure modes as first-class evaluation signals in agentic industrial workflows. Rather than treating failure as a binary outcome, AssetOpsBench analyzes full multi-agent execution trajectories to identify where, how, and why agent behavior breaks down under realistic operational constraints.

Failure analysis in AssetOpsBench is implemented through a dedicated trajectory-level pipeline (TrajFM), which combines LLM-based reasoning with statistical clustering to surface interpretable failure patterns from agent execution traces. This pipeline operates in three stages: (1) trajectory-level failure extraction using an LLM-guided diagnostic prompt, (2) embedding-based clustering to group recurring failure patterns, and (3) analysis and visualization to support developer feedback and iteration.

Across industrial scenarios, recurrent failure modes include:.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, AssetOpsBench does not rely solely on a fixed, hand-crafted failure taxonomy. While a structured set of predefined failure categories (e.g., verification errors, step repetition, role violations) is used for consistency, the system is explicitly designed to discover newly introduced failure patterns that emerge in practice. Additional failure modes identified by the LLM are embedded and clustered automatically, allowing the taxonomy to evolve as new agent designs and behaviors are evaluated.

To preserve industrial confidentiality, raw execution traces are never exposed. Instead, agents receive aggregated scores across six evaluation dimensions together with clustered failure-mode summaries that explain why an agent failed, without revealing sensitive data or intermediate reasoning steps. This feedback-driven design enables developers to diagnose weaknesses, refine agent workflows, and iteratively resubmit improved agents.

This failure-aware evaluation reflects the realities of industrial asset management, where cautious, degradation-aware reasoning—and the ability to recognize uncertainty, defer action, or escalate appropriately—is often preferable to aggressive but brittle automation.

It has been revealed that assetOpsBench-Live is designed as an open, competition-ready benchmark, and we welcome submissions of agent implementations from the community. Agents are evaluated in a controlled, privacy-preserving environment that reflects real industrial asset management constraints.

To submit an agent, developers first validate their implementation locally using a provided simulated environment, which includes representative sensor data, work orders, alerts, and failure-mode catalogs. Agents are then containerized and submitted for remote execution on hidden evaluation scenarios.

Submitted agents are evaluated across six qualitative dimensions—task completion, accuracy, result verification, action sequencing, clarity, and hallucination—using a consistent, reproducible evaluation protocol. Execution traces are not exposed; instead, participants receive aggregated scores and structured failure-mode feedback that highlights where and why an agent’s reasoning or coordination broke down.

Industry observers note that this feedback-driven evaluation loop enables iterative improvement: developers can diagnose failure patterns, refine agent design or workflow structure, and resubmit updated agents for further evaluation. Both planning-focused and execution-focused agents are supported, allowing researchers and practitioners to explore diverse agentic designs within the same benchmark framework.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, every SSL certificate comes with a limited lifespan. Following the latest enhancement from the CA/Browser Forum, the maximum lifetime of a certificate has fallen from 398 days to 200, and it will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Renewal is no longer an annual chore. It’s an ongoing task that only stays manageable with automation.

Industry observers note that so what does this mean if you already look after sites with SSL certificates, and will it bring drastic changes? For many setups, very little will change. For others, one missed renewal can mean an outage. This article explains what’s changing and what to do if you’re in the second group.

Today, an SSL certificate is valid for 200 days at most. The limit applies when a certificate is issued, so the ones you already hold keep their original expiration date.

Where you feel it depends on how your certificates renew. Sites on managed hosting platforms or behind a content delivery network (CDN) usually renew automatically already, often every 90 days, so the new limit changes little. The pressure lands on setups where someone buys a certificate once a year and installs it by hand. At 47 days, that becomes about 12 renewals a year.

Industry observers note that A certificate is a promise from a certificate authority that a key really belongs to a domain, and that promise gets less reliable the longer it runs. If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, it stays usable until it expires. Cutting the lifetime shrinks that window, so a problem that once lingered for over a year is now fixed in weeks.

Shorter lifetimes also make revocation, the process for canceling a bad certificate, far less critical. Revocation has never worked perfectly, but a certificate that expires within weeks matters much less if a cancellation doesn’t reach every browser.

Sources indicate that another reason is about people. A task done once a year is easy to forget and hard to check from outside. Browser makers have pushed for years to move the industry onto automatic renewal, on the logic that a process that runs every few weeks gets tested constantly. If it breaks, you notice swiftly instead of discovering it on the day the certificate expires.

For most people, the first effect is simply more work. A certificate that once needed attention every year will soon need it every few weeks. Plus, each renewal is a small chance for something to go wrong. Multiply that by dozens of sites, mail servers, and devices, and the chance of one slipping through grows promptly.

The safety nets are also thinner. If you relied on the renewal emails, nothing is watching your certificates now. Additionally, with a shorter life, there’s less time between this should have renewed and this has expired.

Recent findings suggest that an expired certificate doesn’t make a site slow or dated. It makes it unreachable for most visitors. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all show a full-page warning that the connection isn’t private, and most people leave instead of clicking through. If the site uses HSTS, a setting that tells browsers to connect only over secure links, there is often no way to click through at all, and visitors are blocked outright until the certificate is fixed.

Recent findings suggest that the damage doesn’t stop at the home page. Checkouts, contact forms, and logins that depend on the secure connection fail along with it, often without an error message that points at the real cause. Other systems break, too, because apps and integrations that call your site over a secure link refuse to connect to an expired certificate.

According to recent reports, nothing about your site has to change for any of this to happen. A date passes, and a site that worked on Friday is down on Monday. In a 47-day lifetime, that date comes around about every six weeks.

Automatic renewal tools do the heavy lifting well. The failures happen around them:.

Industry observers note that look at the five failures above and you’ll see what they share. Each one happens quietly. The renewal job ran, or looked like it did, and nobody checked what the server was actually serving afterwards. Automation can tell you it tried. It can’t tell you the result reached your visitors.

Recent findings suggest that what closes that gap is a check that never relies on your server’s own account of events. Site24x7’s SSL/TLS certificate monitoring does exactly that. It reads the certificate installed on your web server from the cloud, the way a visitor’s browser would, and alerts you before it expires, using thresholds you choose. If a renewal fails quietly, you hear about it from the monitor and not from a customer.

For each certificate, it records the issuing authority, the owner, the matter date, the expiration date, and the days remaining, including on servers that host several certificates behind one address. That last number matters more as lifespans shrink. When a certificate lasts 47 days, the days left is the figure that tells you a renewal is overdue, and you can set your warning against it using the quarter-of-the-lifetime rule covered next.

Once a monitor is watching your certificates, the next question is when it should speak up.

Most expiration alerts are set to a fixed number of days: warn at 30 days left and escalate at seven. That works for a certificate that lasts a year and renews with a month to spare. It breaks when the whole certificate lasts for a limited number of days.

Here’s why: a healthy certificate renews with about a third of its life still left. If your alert appears earlier than that, it goes off on certificates that are doing nothing wrong, and soon everyone ignores it. As lifespans shrink, a fixed 30-day alert will start doing exactly that.

The fix is to set the alerts based on lateness, not on how close the expiry date is. Warn when a quarter of the lifetime is left, since a renewal is overdue by then, and escalate when a tenth is left. Because these are shares of the lifetime, they keep working, however short lifespans get.

The next cut lands on March 15, 2027, so a few checks now will save you from scrambling later:.

Shorter lifespans won’t break your site, but a missed renewal will, so fix the quiet failures now while a mistake still costs an afternoon to fix, not a Monday morning outage affecting lots of customers.

  • “Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the AI industry is doing in spades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”? Fret over the threat of “superintelligence”? How about call an AI assistant your “co-pilot”? Beware: you may have been glosslit by the AI industry. “Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the AI industry is doing in spades. Every industry has its own specialized vocab, and there’s nothing inherently wrong with insider lingo. But with an industry like AI, where development is hotly debated and potential controversy lies around every corner, word choice around the industry takes on extra weight. What is glosslighting? For the study, researchers analyzed 30 of the AI industry’s biggest buzzwords, breaking down the ways that common language around the technology can control public opinion. The study’s authors emphasize that while AI terms have been looked at in isolation, they’re more interested in AI’s “interlocking vocabulary” and the way it protects AI companies from taking accountability for the dark sides of their technology. “Behind the language of seamless intelligence are workers who classify traumatic content for low wages, communities whose water is consumed by server farms, and individuals whose lives are determined by probabilistic decision tools sometimes named, reassuringly, as ‘solutions,'” the authors write. How AI jargon causes harm The study’s authors group the terms by the way they cause harm, the truth about AI they obscure, and the questions they deflect. Those groupings include the following: “Hallucination,” “co-pilot,” “robot rights,” and “agentic AI” humanize the technology, diverting attention from the people and companies making the decisions around them “The cloud,” “data mining,” “scaling,” and “human-in-the-loop” hide the environmental and social costs of AI development “Superintelligence,” “frontier AI,” “AGI,” “existential risk,” “smart city,” “AI superpower,” and “race to AI” shift focus to the future of AI, limiting attention on present-day concerns “Democratizing AI,” “open AI,” “responsible AI,” “ethical AI,” “collaborative AI,” and “human-centric AI” let AI companies frame themselves as trustworthy “Bias,” “ex-ante risk regulation,” “deep learning,” and “data subjects” paint some problems as technological or too complex for laymen to understand, shutting down debates about their usage before they begin The study’s authors go on to recommend alternatives for many of these terms that either simplify communication, demystify confusing terms, or go more in-depth to provide greater accuracy to AI’s impact. One author, assistant professor of computing science Nicholas Vincent, told Tech Xplore that “challenges where there’s real complexity mean there’s a responsibility to do more to help people understand.” “Everyone exposed to AI deserves accurate descriptions of what it is and how it’s used,” Vincent said. “As consumers get a little bit pickier, there’s going to be more demand for specifics. That is, ‘If you want me to buy your expensive AI product, you better have a pretty clear sales pitch for what it actually is.’”.

Unlocking Agentic RL Training for GPT-OSS: A Practical Retrospective

📅 27 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) extends traditional LLM training by optimizing not just a single-turn response, but an entire decision-making process learned through direct interaction with an environment during training.
  • LinkedIn is an AI-first firm that's built agents to help professionals be more successful.
  • The GPT-OSS model has shown comparable performance to OpenAI o3-mini and o4-mini [ref], but its suitability for agentic reinforcement learning training has not yet been validated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) extends traditional LLM training by optimizing not just a single-turn response, but an entire decision-making process learned through direct interaction with an environment during training. Unlike traditional single-turn reinforcement learning or offline preference-based methods that rely on static datasets, agentic RL trains policies by actively collecting on-policy data as the agent looks actions, invokes tools, observes outcomes, and adapts its behavior over multi-step trajectories in either simulated or real environments. This interaction-driven optimization assigns credit across long-horizon decisions, where intermediate choices such as query reformulation, tool selection, and execution order directly influence downstream success. Training follows an iterative closed loop in which the agent interacts with the environment to collect rollout trajectories, computes rewards over these trajectories, updates the policy based on observed outcomes, and then uses the updated policy to drive the next round of interaction and data collection such as GRPO or PPO algorithms..

LinkedIn is an AI-first firm that's built agents to help professionals be more successful. In this setting, models must reason over incomplete information, interact with structured services, and adapt to evolving user intent across multiple steps rather than produce a single static response. These capabilities are especially critical for agents that support the goals of recruiters, job and knowledge seekers, and learners end users, such as retrieving information, refining queries, coordinating tools, and executing multi-step workflows. By learning robust decision policies through interaction, agentic RL provides a principled foundation for building scalable, reliable, and adaptable AI systems through end-to-end optimization.

The GPT-OSS model has shown comparable performance to OpenAI o3-mini and o4-mini [ref], but its suitability for agentic reinforcement learning training has not yet been validated. Most recent work focuses on fine-tuning without tool calling, such as: Fine-tuning with gpt-oss and Hugging Face Transformers and unsloth tutorial: how to fine-tune gpt-oss. This blog explores the journey to unlock agentic RL training for GPT-OSS as a potential backbone model for agentic applications.

It has been revealed that in our experiments, we use verl as our training framework since it is one of the most popular adopted frameworks in the open source community. We use gsm8k, Retool task, verifiable instruction following task, which are commonly used in RL training. We focus on presenting experimental results for the GPT-OSS-20B model, and our attention-sink fix also works for GPT-OSS-120B. The Qwen-2.5-32B model is additionally used to benchmark standard metric trends during RL training.

verl has been an OSS framework used by the team, and the team has previously collaborated and contributed to it to help democratize agentic reinforcement learning training. With the introduction of the fresh Harmony chat template in GPT-OSS, the first step is to ensure that the training framework fully supports the updated message format and conversation semantics required by Harmony. This step helps rollout generation, trajectory construction, and tool parsing remain consistent and correct under the new template.

In a recent development, the team uses ReTool as a representative example to verify code correctness. ReTool is an agentic coding task in which the model is asked to solve a math problem with the assistance of a code compiler tool. This setup allows the model to focus on core reasoning and algorithmic logic, while delegating the actual arithmetic and execution to the tool. During an episode, the model interacts with the code tool multiple times, using execution results as feedback to refine its solution. At the end of the trajectory, the model produces a final answer, on which the reward is computed.

During the initial training runs, we observed exploding KL divergence and entropy, along with non-increasing rewards, indicating underlying issues in the GPT-OSS training setup, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Left: Qwen32b has significantly higher rewards compared to GPT-OSS 20B; Right: The gradient norm exploded as training progressed.

Industry observers note that figure 2. Non-zero importance sampling clip value even for on-policy training.

It has been revealed that we focus on on-policy methods because they provide greater stability and more reliable convergence. The foundation of pure on-policy Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) mandates that the importance sampling ratio must be exactly 1. The mathematical definition of the importance ratio is:.

ratio=π(a∣s)πold(a∣s) \text{ratio} = \frac{\pi(a \mid s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)} ratio=πold​(a∣s)π(a∣s)​.

This requirement ensures that the policy update is executed only on the data generated by the current policy π(a | s) = πold(a | s), preventing unintended clipping.

We have observed the non-zero clipping value in our ReTool training, as shown in Figure 2, stemming from a mismatch between the two log-probabilities:.

Root Cause: The Dual Forward Pass and MoE Architecture.

Prior to verl 0.3.0, the implementation relied on two separate forward passes (one to compute the current log_prob and one to retrieve the stored old_log_prob) for the same state-action pair.

In a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture like GPT-OSS, the gating network routes the input to different experts. Due to implementation factors (e.g., subtle floating-point differences or explicit stochasticity), the expert routing can differ slightly between the two passes. Readers who are interested can further read Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers.

This difference in routing leads to:.

log⁡(π(a∣s))≠log⁡(πold(a∣s)) \log(\pi(a \mid s)) \neq \log(\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)) log(π(a∣s))=log(πold​(a∣s)).

The resulting ratio deviates from 1, falsely triggering the PPO clip and violating the core on-policy assumption.

Solution: Enforcing Ratio = 1 via Log-Probability Substitution.

The fix resolves the glitch by logically overriding the flawed computation when the environment is known to be on-policy (i.e., when the minibatch size equals the global batch size):.

By setting old_log_prob equal to the newly computed log_prob (detached to prevent gradient flow through the reference value), the importance ratio is mathematically forced back to 1. This strategy bypasses the instability caused by MoE's non-deterministic routing and guarantees strict on-policy behavior during PPO training.

Recent findings suggest that although fixing the log-probability mismatch reduced the importance-sampling clip ratio to zero, gradient norms continued to explode and rewards failed to improve. To isolate the glitch, we simplified training to GSM8K, a single-step task without agentic tool use. The same instability persisted, as shown in the green curves in Figure 3, indicating a fundamental issue in basic RL training with GPT-OSS under verl.

We hypothesize that training–inference mismatch could be a potential cause: discrepancies between inference-time execution—where engines such as vLLM and SGLang aggressively optimize for throughput—and training-time execution under FSDP, which prioritizes numerical precision and stability, can effectively turn otherwise on-policy RL into off-policy optimization.

According to recent reports, this blog details why such mismatches lead to unstable gradients and non-improving rewards. Figure 3 compares training runs with and without rollout correction (see this verl blog for details). After applying rollout correction, training dynamics improve significantly, with gradient norms remaining stable rather than exploding.

However, as shown in the left plot of Figure 4, the reward increases only modestly, and convergence on the simple GSM8K task remains substantially slower compared to smaller dense model variants.

It has been revealed that figure 3. Gradient norm behavior under different training configurations. Green: Training without rollout correction, exhibiting unstable gradients. Red: Training with the attention layer frozen to isolate the matter to the attention mechanism, resulting in partial stabilization. Blue: Training with rollout correction enabled (sequence-level importance sampling), yielding stable gradient norms.

According to recent reports, figure 4. Left: Reward improvement on GSM8K remains slow even after applying rollout correction, with performance comparable to runs where the attention layer is frozen during training. Right: A substantial log-ppl mismatch is observed between the inference engine (SGLang with Triton kernels supporting attention-sink forward passes) and the training stack (FSDP with FlashAttention-v2), indicating a large training–inference inconsistency.

It has been revealed that to further isolate the root cause, we freeze the attention layers during training and observe reward dynamics similar to those of runs without freezing (blue curve vs yellow curve in Figure 4). This indicates that learning is primarily driven by the MoE layers, while the attention mechanism contributes less effectively than expected. In addition, we observe a substantial token-level probability mismatch between the inference engine and the distributed training stack which are using different attention kernels. Together, these observations motivate a deeper investigation into the attention mechanism.

Attention sinks used in GPT-OSS are learnable scalar parameters (one per attention head) that act as "virtual tokens" in the softmax computation. They allow the model to allocate attention mass to a learned sink rather than forcing all attention to content tokens, which has been shown to improve attention stability in streaming inference and training with sliding-window attention.

After a deeper investigation, we identified several major problems:.

Key difference: The sink participates in softmax normalization but doesn't contribute to the output.

The attention weight for content token j in row i is defined as:.

Pij=exp⁡(Sij)∑j′=1Nkexp⁡(Sij′)+exp⁡(Sh) P_{ij} = \frac{\exp(S_{ij})} {\sum_{j'=1}^{N_k} \exp(S_{ij'}) + \exp(S_h)} Pij​=∑j′=1Nk​​exp(Sij′​)+exp(Sh​)exp(Sij​)​.

The sink probability is computed but not used in the output:.

Pi,h=exp⁡(Sh)∑j′=1Nkexp⁡(Sij′)+exp⁡(Sh) P_{i,h} = \frac{\exp(S_h)} {\sum_{j'=1}^{N_k} \exp(S_{ij'}) + \exp(S_h)} Pi,h​=∑j′=1Nk​​exp(Sij′​)+exp(Sh​)exp(Sh​)​.

The gradient of the loss L with respect to the sink parameter Sh is:.

∂L∂Sh=−∑iPi,h(∂L∂Si,h−∑j∈{1,…,Nk}Pij∂L∂Sij) \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_h} = - \sum_i P_{i,h} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{i,h}} - \sum_{j \in \{1,\ldots,N_k\}} P_{ij} \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ij}} \right) ∂Sh​∂L​=−i∑​Pi,h​​∂Si,h​∂L​−j∈{1,…,Nk​}∑​Pij​∂Sij​∂L​​.

Since the sink is computed but not used in the output, its gradient ∂L/∂Si,h = 0.

Therefore, the backward equation simplifies to:.

∂L∂Sh=−∑iPi,h(∑j∈{1,…,Nk}Pij∂L∂Sij) \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_h} = - \sum_i P_{i,h} \left( \sum_{j \in \{1,\ldots,N_k\}} P_{ij} \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ij}} \right) ∂Sh​∂L​=−i∑​Pi,h​​j∈{1,…,Nk​}∑​Pij​∂Sij​∂L​​.

Sources indicate that the forward pass was adapted from vLLM's FlashAttention fork, and we implemented the backward pass to compute gradients for the sink parameters. The implementation will be released following the internal review process.

Industry observers note that after applying the fix in FlashAttention v3, we observe substantially faster convergence for GPT-OSS-20B across a range of reinforcement learning tasks. These include single-turn RL on math reasoning (GSM8K — red curve in Figure 5), instruction following (VerifyIf, evaluated on an out-of-domain multi-if benchmark — Figure 6), and multi-turn agentic RL with tool use (ReTool — Figure 7).

Across all settings, training becomes stable and exhibits steady reward improvement.

It has been revealed that figure 5.. Single Turn GSM8K, the red curve converges much faster than the rest without the fix.

Recent findings suggest that figure 6. On verifiable instruction following the task, the run without the fix collapsed (blue), and the run with fix highlighted steady reward improvement.

Sources indicate that figure 7. On the Retool task, the run with fix demonstrated steady reward improvement and no gradient exploding (fa2 is the flash attention 2 without the fix while fa3 is the flash attention 3 with the fix). After the fix, the validation accuracy score goes up now.

One glitch we consistently encountered was excessive memory allocation during the FSDP forward pass, which led to repeated out-of-memory (OOM) failures when training GPT-OSS-20B bf16 models on 16 H200 nodes (max response length: 16k, prompt length: 8k). This behavior is highly unexpected for a 20B-parameter MoE model.

Recent findings suggest that we identified the problem as originating from two different implementations of the MoE forward path in Hugging Face Transformers. This issue has also been reported by other people: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/problems/40073; When verl computes log-probabilities under FSDP, the inference forward path is triggered. In the current Hugging Face implementation, this path duplicates hidden states for all experts and performs batched matrix multiplication, materializing extremely large tensors in GPU memory. By contrast, the training forward path uses a for-loop to process each expert sequentially and then combines the results. While slower, this approach is significantly more memory efficient.

We patched the Hugging Face implementation to use a more memory-efficient execution path, avoiding repeated materialization of experts.

Agentic RL requires the agent to interact with the environment over multiple steps while maintaining an ever-expanding context. Observations and environment feedback from each step are appended to the context and used as input for subsequent decision-making, which introduces significant challenges for memory efficiency and scalability during training.

Under fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), model parameters, optimizer states, and gradients are sharded across the entire world size (i.e., all GPUs in the training cluster). Each GPU stores and updates only its assigned parameter shards, while rollout data are replicated across all GPUs—meaning every GPU processes the full agent interaction history for each rollout.

During the forward pass, when computation reaches a layer whose parameters are not locally available, an all_gather operation is triggered to materialize the full parameters across GPUs. During the backward pass, a corresponding reduce_scatter operation aggregates gradients and ensures that each GPU retains only its local shard. This provides a degree of scaling: as the number of GPUs increases, the per-GPU memory footprint decreases.

Industry observers note that FSDP provides model-level scaling by sharding model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs. Sequence parallelism (or context parallelism) further reduces per-GPU memory consumption by partitioning the input sequence across devices, thereby lowering the peak activation memory on each GPU.

Industry observers note that as the number of sequence-parallel dimensions increases, the maximum activation memory per GPU correspondingly decreases. We have implemented sequence parallelism to be attention-sink-aware and compatible with FlashAttention v3 (Figure 8, right).

Recent findings suggest that figure 8. Left: Inference without sequence parallelism. Right: Inference with sequence parallelism, where additional all-to-all communication is performed before and after the attention layer. This partitions the sequence across parallel workers and reduces the peak memory footprint of attention computation by a factor proportional to the sequence-parallelism degree.

Recent findings suggest that sequence parallelism scales along the sequence dimension to reduce the per-GPU activation footprint. Input tokens from all sequences are packed into a single contiguous list by removing padding tokens, while position IDs are used to distinguish tokens belonging to different sequences. This design naturally benefits from FlashAttention’s variable-length support. For sequence parallelism, layers other than the attention layer do not have inter-position dependencies; therefore, they do not require each GPU to hold a complete sequence shard, and no additional communication is needed for these layers.

It has been revealed that the attention layer, however, requires all tokens belonging to the same sequence to be present on the same GPU in order to compute attention weights correctly. To satisfy this constraint, an all-to-all communication is performed to gather sequence elements, with the split performed at the attention-head level. This design avoids communication within the attention computation itself, which would otherwise be prohibitively expensive. After the attention layer, a single all-to-all communication redistributes the outputs back to their original sequence-parallel layout, after which the remaining non-attention layers can proceed without further synchronization.

Our journey to enable agentic RL training for the GPT-OSS backbone model was a practical retrospective, highlighting that unlocking advanced capabilities in open-source LLMs requires meticulous, deep-dive engineering.

We made contributions that transformed the viability of GPT-OSS for agentic applications, specifically by:.

Stabilizing PPO: We contributed a fix to restore on-policy integrity, overriding the log-probability mismatch caused by the MoE architecture’s non-determinism (Figure 2).

Enabling Attention Sink Support: We successfully implemented and integrated the attention sink backward pass into FlashAttention v3, correcting the catastrophic training–inference mismatch that had previously caused instability and slow convergence (Figures 5, 6, and 7).

Scaling Memory Efficiency: We introduced crucial memory optimizations, including patching the MoE materialization process and integrating sequence parallelism with the new attention sink support, enabling training with the long context windows essential for multi-step agents (Figure 8).

These engineering efforts validate GPT-OSS as a scalable and high-performance backbone for building the next generation of intelligent, multi-step decision-making agents.

Thanks to Deepak Agarwal, Bee-Chung Chen, Animesh Singh, Gungor Polatkan, Balaji Krishnapuram, and Jitendra Agarwal for their leadership support.

Recent findings suggest that thank you for this detailed retrospective on enabling agentic RL training for GPT-OSS. The article clearly documents important challenges and practical solutions. I have a few questions and observations that might help clarify some aspects.

Mathematical Clarification on Attention Sink Gradient.

It has been revealed that regarding the attention sink backward pass derivation (Section 4), I'd appreciate clarification on the notation and justification. The article presents the general formula: ∂L/∂S_h = -Σ_i P_{i,h} (∂L/∂S_{i,h} - Σ_{j∈{1,...,N_k}} P_{ij} ∂L/∂S_{ij}). Then states that ∂L/∂S_{i,h} = 0 because "the sink is computed but not used in the output," leading to the simplified form: ∂L/∂S_h = -Σ_i P_{i,h} (Σ_j P_{ij} ∂L/∂S_{ij}).

It has been revealed that I believe the final formula is correct, but the notation ∂L/∂S_{i,h} is unclear. If this refers to the gradient of the loss with respect to the sink's contribution to the output at position i (i.e., ∂L/∂(P_{i,h} V_sink)), then indeed it would be zero since there's no V_sink term. However, the sink parameter S_h itself does affect the output through softmax normalization: P_{ij} = exp(S_{ij}) / (Σ_{j'} exp(S_{ij'}) + exp(S_h)). When S_h changes, all P_{ij} change, affecting O_i = Σ_j P_{ij} V_j. The gradient ∂L/∂S_h is non-zero and flows through this normalization.

Could you clarify what ∂L/∂S_{i,h} represents in your notation? Also, could you provide the full derivation showing how you arrive at the final form from the chain rule through the softmax operation? A step-by-step derivation would help readers verify the implementation and understand how the gradient flows through the attention mechanism.

On-Policy Fix: Clarification Needed.

Industry observers note that the solution for the MoE log-probability mismatch (Section 2) sets old_log_prob = log_prob.detach() when on_policy=True. While this mathematically forces the importance sampling ratio to 1, I'm curious about the implications. If the policy parameters change between rollout collection and the training step (even slightly), this fix would still assume ratio = 1. How do you ensure true on-policy conditions? Do you collect rollouts and train in the same step, or is there a mechanism to detect policy drift?

Have you considered storing the actual routing decisions during rollout to ensure deterministic replay, or using deterministic routing during training? This might address the root cause rather than working around it. Also, the fix only applies when on_policy=True. How do you handle cases where the policy has drifted? Is there a threshold or mechanism to detect when to switch to off-policy mode?

Recent findings suggest that several aspects would benefit from additional detail. Which fix had the largest impact? Are all three fixes necessary, or would fixing attention sinks alone have been sufficient? A table showing results with/without each fix would be very helpful. You mention the fixes work for GPT-OSS-120B, but no experimental results are shown. Could you share learning curves or metrics for the 120B model?

The article mentions both vLLM and SGLang. Which engine is used for rollouts in the final experiments? If different engines are used for different experiments, how does this affect the training-inference mismatch analysis? You also reference "rollout correction (sequence-level importance sampling)" and mention "this verl blog," but the details aren't explained. Could you clarify what this correction does and how it relates to the attention sink fix?

Implementation and Reproducibility.

The article mentions that "The implementation will be released following the internal review process." For reproducibility and verification, it would be valuable to know an approximate timeline for release, whether the backward pass implementation will be contributed to the main FlashAttention repository, and if there are any interim workarounds or partial implementations that could be shared.

Despite these questions, the article makes valuable contributions. It clearly identifies real-world challenges with MoE + RL training, documents the engineering journey transparently, shows substantial improvements in training stability, and raises awareness of training-inference mismatch issues. The fixes appear to work well for your use case, and the results demonstrate clear improvements. My questions are aimed at understanding the details better and ensuring the solutions are robust and reproducible.

Thank you again for sharing this work with the community!

Latest Update: AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang is back at Nvidia.
  • On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis.
  • Recent findings suggest that investors may be relieved to have Huang back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis. Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board noted it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has revealed additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns. Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him. Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN. The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses. Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait? Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it. “AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.” AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology. THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker. Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise? Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players. “Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub notes. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.” Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products. “The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.” That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on. In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan showed how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve customers as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices. Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing. “The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says. She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning. “I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says. For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations. Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance. THE BILL IS COMING DUE Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology. Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more quickly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save. “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.” Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive. Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost. Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified. The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive. Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with. “Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company. This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each latest generation of frontier models? Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow. “I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.” WHO GETS THE VALUE? Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software. Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods. “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.” His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient. “Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?” Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work. “These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says. Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify. For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most crucial operations. “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary. A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running. And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want. During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.” He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them. WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money. O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models. “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.” But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves. Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies. Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward. AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses. “We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns. Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed. For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them. Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more rapidly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save.

According to recent reports, “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley indicates. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.”.

Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive.

Industry observers note that kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost.

Sources indicate that some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified.

The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can promptly become expensive.

It has been revealed that airia claims its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with.

“Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Firm.

This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each new generation of frontier models?

Industry observers note that companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow.

“I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.”.

Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software.

Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology firm eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods.

According to recent reports, “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.”.

According to recent reports, his tech giant combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient.

“Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen notes. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?”.

Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work.

“These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he states.

Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify.

For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation tech giant Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most important operations.

Industry observers note that “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary.

It has been revealed that A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running.

And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want.

During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.”.

He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them.

A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money.

O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models.

In a recent development, “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she claims. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.”.

But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves.

Industry observers note that ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies.

Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward.

AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses.

“We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns.

According to recent reports, huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the manufacturer with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed.

In a recent development, for much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers declared, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them.

Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

Alyah ⭐️: Toward Robust Evaluation of Emirati Dialect Capabilities in Arabic LLMs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, arabic is one of the most widely spoken languages in the world, with hundreds of millions of speakers across more than twenty countries.
  • Industry observers note that this gap is particularly problematic as large language models increasingly interact with people in informal, culturally grounded, and conversational settings.
  • The Emirati dialect is deeply intertwined with local culture, heritage, and history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📦 Dataset on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.

According to recent reports, arabic is one of the most widely spoken languages in the world, with hundreds of millions of speakers across more than twenty countries. Despite this global reach, Arabic is not a monolithic language. Modern Standard Arabic coexists with a rich landscape of regional dialects that differ significantly in vocabulary, syntax, phonology, and cultural grounding. These dialects are the primary medium of daily communication, oral storytelling, poetry, and social interaction. However, most existing benchmarks for Arabic large language models focus almost exclusively on Modern Standard Arabic, leaving dialectal Arabic largely under-evaluated and under-represented.

Industry observers note that this gap is particularly problematic as large language models increasingly interact with people in informal, culturally grounded, and conversational settings. A model that performs well on formal newswire text may still fail to understand a greeting, an idiomatic expression, or a short anecdote expressed in a local dialect. To address this limitation, our team introduces Alyah الياه (which means North Star ⭐️ in Emirati), an Emirati-centric benchmark designed to assess how well Arabic LLMs capture the linguistic, cultural, and pragmatic aspects of the Emirati dialect.

The Emirati dialect is deeply intertwined with local culture, heritage, and history. It appears in everyday greetings, oral poetry, proverbs, folk narratives, and expressions whose meanings cannot be inferred through literal translation alone. Our benchmark is intentionally designed to probe this depth. Rather than testing surface-level lexical knowledge, it challenges models on their ability to interpret culturally embedded meaning, pragmatic usage, and dialect-specific nuances.

The benchmark covers a wide range of content, including common and uncommon local expressions, culturally grounded greetings, short anecdotes, heritage-related questions, and references to Emirati poetry. The goal is not only to measure correctness, but also to understand where models systematically succeed or fail when confronted with authentic Emirati language use.

According to recent reports, following further development and consolidation, the benchmark has been unified into a single dataset called Alyah. The final benchmark contains 1,173 samples, all collected manually from native Emirati speakers to ensure linguistic authenticity and cultural grounding. This manual curation step was essential to capture expressions, meanings, and usages that are rarely documented in written resources and are difficult to infer from Modern Standard Arabic alone.

Each sample is formulated as a multiple-choice question with four candidate answers, exactly one of which is correct. Large language models were used to synthetically generate the distractor choices, after which they were reviewed to ensure plausibility and semantic closeness to the correct answer. To avoid positional bias during evaluation, the index of the correct answer follows a randomized distribution across the dataset. Below is the distribution of word count per query and candidate answers.

Industry observers note that alyah spans a broad spectrum of linguistic and cultural phenomena in the Emirati dialect, ranging from everyday expressions to culturally sensitive and figurative language. The distribution across categories is summarized below.

Below are examples of each category:.

This composition allows Alyah to jointly evaluate surface-level conversational fluency and deeper cultural, semantic, and pragmatic understanding, with a particular emphasis on dialect-specific language phenomena that remain challenging for current models.

Sources indicate that we evaluated a total of 54 language models, comprising 23 base models and 31 instruction-tuned models, spanning several architectural and training paradigms. These include Arabic-native LLMs such as Jais and Allam, multilingual models with strong Arabic support such as Qwen and LLaMA, and adapted or regionally specialized models such as Fanar and AceGPT. For each family, both base and instruction-tuned variants were evaluated in order to understand the impact of alignment and instruction tuning on dialectal performance.

All models were evaluated under a consistent prompting and scoring protocol. Responses were assessed for semantic correctness and appropriateness with respect to Emirati usage, rather than literal overlap with a reference answer. This is particularly important for dialectal evaluation, where multiple valid phrasings may exist.

For each question category, we estimated difficulty empirically based on model performance. Categories where most models struggled were labeled as harder, while those consistently answered correctly across model families were considered easier. This approach allows difficulty to emerge from observed behavior rather than from subjective annotation alone.

In a recent development, we evaluate a broad set of contemporary Arabic and multilingual large language models on Alyah, using accuracy on multiple-choice questions as the primary metric. The evaluation covers 53 models in total, including 22 base models and 31 instruction-tuned models, spanning Arabic-native, multilingual, and regionally adapted systems. Below is a radar plot showing the performance of top models of different sizes per question category.

These results are intended as reference measurements within the scope of Alyah, rather than absolute rankings across all Arabic benchmarks.

According to recent reports, several trends emerge from the evaluation. Instruction-tuned models generally outperform their base counterparts as shown in Figures 1 and 2. This is particularly the case on questions involving conversational norms and culturally appropriate responses (i.e. the Etiquette & Values Category). Furthermore, it is the case with questions that test imagery and figurative meaning. This can be attributed, to the model’s original strong capabilities with understanding MSA-based imagery and figurative language regardless of the dialect at hand. The models are able to draw patterns of non-literal description regardless of dialect. Generally, the most difficult categories for the models were consistently “Language and Dialect” and “Greeting and Daily expressions” across model sizes as shown in figure 1. These results reflect the current state of Emirati dialect presence in written media, as the dialect is mostly spoken rarely written, which explains its novelty relative to the evaluated models. Nonetheless, there is a clear benefit to instruct models with understanding the dialect (and the other evaluation categories) in comparison to their counterparts, especially in small and medium models. This is particularly noticeable with the Poetry and Creative Expression category, which is where the large instruct models performed marginally better than the smaller models.

Industry observers note that as shown in Figure 3, even strong multilingual models show notable degradation on the most challenging Alyah questions, suggesting that dialect-specific semantic knowledge is not easily acquired through generic multilingual training alone. It must be noted that while Arabic-native models tend to perform more robustly on culturally grounded content, their performances are not uniform across all categories (figure 2). In particular, questions involving implicit meanings and rare expressions remain difficult across nearly all evaluated models. This highlights a persistent gap between surface-level dialect familiarity and deeper cultural understanding. The high variance in performance across categories , where a model that excels at imagery and figurative meaning may still struggle with poetry or heritage-related creative questions, indicates that dialectal competence is multi-dimensional and cannot be captured by a single score. Figure 3 demonstrates that the highest scoring large model in Jais-2-70B, followed by the two small models jais-2-8B and ALLaM-7B-instruct, which are all Arabic instruct-tuned models.

This benchmark represents a step toward more realistic and culturally grounded evaluation of Arabic language models. By focusing on the Emirati dialect, we aim to support the development of models that better serve local communities, institutions, and consumers in the UAE. Beyond model ranking, the benchmark is intended as a diagnostic tool to guide future data collection, training, and adaptation efforts.

It has been revealed that we invite researchers, practitioners, and the broader community to use the benchmark, explore the results, and share feedback. Community input will be essential to refining the dataset, expanding coverage, and ensuring that dialectal Arabic receives the attention it deserves in the evaluation of Large Language Models.
